newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African arms industry says it crippled by cuts.
newsitem.headline: S.African arms industry says it crippled by cuts.

text.p: South Africa's arms industry has laid off hundreds of workers in recent weeks and is losing its technical edge because of deep budget cuts, industry sources said on Thursday.
"It's almost at crisis point," said Jakes Abba Omar, spokesman for the state weapons agency Armscor.
He said the industry was feeling the effects of defence budget cuts ordered this year by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, who has pledged to keep state spending on a tight rein.
Defence Minister Joe Modise has asked Deputy President Thabo Mbeki to intervene on his behalf in a dispute with Manuel over a 1.4 billion rand cut in the 1997/98 defence budget.
Nelson Mandela's cabinet on Wednesday approved a broad review of South Africa's defence needs which fits closely with Modise's view, but the review does not guarantee any extra funds will be found.
One of the drafters of the review, Laurie Nathan, said that purchase of any equipment proposed in the document -- such as four naval corvettes -- would still depend on budget constraints.
"The review represents an ideal model," he said, adding that it did not specify whether equipment should be bought abroad or from local manufacturers.
Armscor sources said buying corvettes as part of a package offered by Britain, which has been mooted by the South African defence ministry, could further marginalise the local industry.
"Over the past few months there's been a slow but growing white-anting process, a hollowing out, where bits and pieces of the industry have been imploding," one source said.

"It's very serious. From 1989 to 1997 we've moved from being part of space-age technology to now being at the level of towed artillery systems. That's the highest level of technology our defence industry is capable of at the moment," the source said.
"A further cut would mean that we go below that, so we go into producing explosives, a few guns."
The sources said at least 800 workers had been laid off in recent weeks by defence firms. The only companies coping were those with export orders.
Executives at Denel, the country's biggest arms maker, describe the weapons industry as South Africa's most successful manufacturing sector.

The industry owes much of its success to international sanctions during the apartheid years, when South Africa was forced to design and build its own arms or modify technology obtained clandestinely from other countries.
Denel issued a statement on Thursday saying it was still committed to its flagship Rooivalk combat helicopter project despite the cuts in the defence budget.

Modise had told parliament that this was one of the projects under threat from the budget cuts, because the South African Air Force might not be able to go through with a plan to buy about a dozen of the aircraft.
"Denel understands the government's commitment to social reconstruction which inevitably involves a review and prioritisation of the budget," the Denel statement said.
"It is Denel's understanding that rationalisation will be facilitated through hi-tech military technology for which Denel has become reputable."

Manuel is currently out of the country. His cuts to the defence budget are approved by many members of the ruling African National Congress, who feel any money spent on guns could be better spent on housing, health or education.
